title: Noise-Robust Spin-Orbit Qubit in Germanium Holes via p-Orbital Encoding
abstract: Germanium hole spin qubits are a leading platform for semiconductor quantum computation due to their strong spin-orbit coupling, all-electrical operability, and absence of valley degeneracy. A central obstacle is charge noise, which couples to the qubit through the same spin-orbit interaction that enables fast electrical control. In this work, we propose a new operational mode of a three-hole quantum dot in a planar Ge/SiGe heterostructure, modeled within a four-band Luttinger-Kohn--Bir-Pikus framework: a spin-$p$-orbital (SpO) qubit encoded in the $p$-shell of the topmost hole. We characterize charge noise sweet spots in the parameter space of electrostatic confinement and magnetic field, and estimate that relaxation rates of the SpO qubit are comparable to those of spin qubits hosted in single holes. We then design and optimize an all-electrical Landau-Zener state-transfer protocol that induces logical qubit state transitions without microwave driving, and we show that the quadrupole-quadrupole Coulomb interaction between neighboring dots enables fast two-qubit entangling gates operated by adiabatic shuttling.
summary: This paper introduces a noise-robust qubit platform using the spin-p-orbital (SpO) manifold in a Germanium hole quantum dot. By operating at specific isotropic points, the qubit's energy splitting becomes insensitive to charge noise fluctuations. The authors further demonstrate the feasibility of implementing fast, high-fidelity quantum gates using purely electrical control techniques like adiabatic shuttling.
main_problem: The primary challenge addressed is mitigating charge noise, a major obstacle for semiconductor quantum computation using Germanium hole qubits.
main_result: The authors propose encoding a qubit in a spin-p-orbital (SpO) manifold, demonstrating robustness against charge noise at specific isotropic operating points and designing all-electrical protocols for fast, high-fidelity quantum gates.
method: The work involves developing an effective Hamiltonian within a four-band Luttinger-Kohn–Bir-Pikus framework, characterizing noise sweet spots, and optimizing gate sequences using adiabatic shuttling and state-transfer protocols.
model_or_system: The system is a three-hole quantum dot fabricated in a planar Ge/SiGe heterostructure. The qubit is encoded in the $p$-shell of the topmost hole, modeled using a Luttinger-Kohn–Bir-Pikus Hamiltonian incorporating strain and electrostatic confinement.

important_parameters: The operating regime is the isotropic point ($\epsilon \approx 0$), and noise levels are targeted around $3 \mu	ext{eV}$ based on material parameters.
main_assumptions: The analysis relies on a shell-filling approximation that treats the lowest two holes as an inert core, and the gate optimization uses a smooth flat-top ansatz.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the energy level structure showing the qubit in the p-shell, the dependence of the qubit splitting on confinement anisotropy ($\epsilon$), and comparisons between different gate optimization techniques (GRAPE vs. flat-top ansatz).
paper_structure: The paper progresses from identifying charge noise as the bottleneck, to proposing the SpO qubit encoding and analyzing its noise robustness via sweet spot characterization. It then details all-electrical gate protocols, including Landau-Zener state transfer and two-qubit entangling gates via adiabatic shuttling.
why_interesting: This work provides a detailed, physics-based blueprint for realizing solid-state qubits, directly addressing noise mitigation and gate implementation using established semiconductor heterostructures, which is highly relevant to quantum computing hardware.
